title: Montaigne close
hook: weeks with a man who wrote about himself and found everyone

segments.voice: Yesterday, what to keep from Montaigne: curiosity, doubt, gentleness, laughter at ourselves. Your line was keep curious. What question did you ask before judging? Day one thousand one hundred eighty-four.

A round tower. Sayings painted on the ceiling beams. A man at a desk, writing down what his runaway mind does when it's left alone. That's where this block began. Since then: a cat who might be playing with him, a fall from a horse that felt softer than he feared, a kidney stone, a mayor who was never quite the same person as Montaigne, and a philosopher who sits on his own bottom like everyone else. He set out to write only about himself. And somehow, readers keep finding themselves in it. Today we close the book.
screen: `A TOWER, A DESK, A RUNAWAY MIND.` → `A CAT, A HORSE, A KIDNEY STONE.` → `HE WROTE ABOUT HIMSELF.`

segments.voice: First, the name. Montaigne called his chapters essais, which in his French means trials, tries, attempts. Not conclusions. He was trying out his judgment on whatever was in front of him, a cannibal, a cat, a cough, and watching what it did. Second, the strange result. He says himself that he is the matter of his book. Yet he also says every person carries the whole form of the human condition. So by looking honestly at one ordinary life, his own, he was looking at everyone's. That's why a reader can open him at random and feel caught. Third, he didn't call it finished. Even after the Essays were printed, he kept adding in the margins, putting a second thought beside the first without striking the first out. The book stayed an attempt. Fourth, the people who came after. Tomorrow this path turns to Ralph Waldo Emerson, an American writer who read Montaigne closely and wrote an essay about him. Of the Essays, Emerson said: "Cut these words, and they would bleed; they are vascular and alive." That's what readers keep finding: not a system to obey, but a living voice that keeps trying. So here are the lines we've carried through this block, a few of them. My tower. The runaway horse. What do I know. Who's playing whom. My own bottom. Haven't I lived. Ordinary pleasures. Keep curious. And now one more, the one Montaigne would hand you: not his attempt, but yours.
screen: `ESSAIS: TRIALS, TRIES, ATTEMPTS.` · `ONE LIFE, THE WHOLE HUMAN CONDITION.` · `HE KEPT ADDING IN THE MARGINS.` · `CUT THESE WORDS, AND THEY WOULD BLEED.` · then, large: `NOT HIS ATTEMPT, BUT YOURS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write your own short essay. Not a long one. A few sentences, on paper, on your phone, or just in your head. Pick a small subject from your own life: how you sleep, a friend, a fear, a habit you can't explain. Begin the way Montaigne might: here is what I notice about it. Then add one honest sentence you wouldn't usually say out loud. Don't polish it. It's an attempt. The bell holds the time.
Montaigne close. The end of our block on a man who tried out his judgment on his own life, and in it found the whole human condition. Today's word.
Your line: my attempt. Today, when something you try comes out rough, call it what Montaigne called his chapters: an attempt, worth keeping and adding to. Day one thousand one hundred eighty-four.

howItsDone: People who love Montaigne often keep a notebook of short, honest pieces about their own lives, written as attempts rather than finished arguments, sometimes adding to old entries years later.

keep it, and add to it in the margins.
turn it into a rule for others.
